A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STAD with the same Gaussian and von Mises-Fisher framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original adaptation experiments on Yearbook, FMoW-Time, and CIFAR-10-C, together with ablation, class-imbalance, representation, and runtime analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations on EVIS, CIFAR-10.1, and ImageNetV2, additional comparisons, and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: The dynamic class-prototype model, Gaussian/vMF formulations, EM inference, and sliding-window adaptation remain unchanged. V2's Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure. Class-specific and fixed concentration options already existed in v1; their experimental configuration changes are assessed under E3.

E1.justification: V2 adds EVIS, covering technological changes in products and vehicles, and the reproduction datasets CIFAR-10.1 and ImageNetV2. Yearbook, FMoW-Time, and CIFAR-10-C remain. This substantially broadens the evaluated domains and shift types, alongside wider evaluation of label-shift scenarios.

E2.justification: SHOT, SAR, LAME, and T3A join BN, TENT, and CoTTA in the retained temporal and CIFAR-10-C comparisons and runtime evaluation. These include directly relevant classifier-adaptation competitors absent from v1. The CIFAR-10-C STAD-vMF+BN row is removed, while temporal BN-combination comparisons are retained and expanded in Appendix D.2.

E3.justification: V2 introduces systematic comparisons between shuffled uniform-label streams and class-ordered label-shift streams, with separate hyperparameter searches. Yearbook uses batches of 2048 for uniform labels and 64 for label shift. For CIFAR-10-C, v1 states initialization of transition concentration at 100, whereas v2 specifies 1000 and fixed concentrations. This establishes a reported setting revision, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds concentration and sliding-window sensitivity studies (Tables 10–11) and a FMoW representation visualization comparing BN and STAD (Figure 7). Batch-size and BN-combination analyses expand across shift settings and datasets. The dynamics ablation and dispersion analysis remain, but v1's fixed-class-proportion Yearbook study and Figure 5 are removed.

E5.justification: V2 Table 5 first reports uncertainty for the static ablation accuracies; v1 Table 2 reported only accuracy differences. Three-training-seed reporting already existed in v1. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, and sensitivity results. For example, under EVIS label shift, LAME scores 69.37% versus STAD-vMF's 62.08%. V1's FMoW STAD accuracy of 86.25% is retained under label shift, while 68.87% is newly reported under uniform labels. Reported FMoW relative runtime changes from 53.3 to 30.8, without sufficient timing details to establish a controlled speedup.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds explicit temporal nonstationarity, bounded divergence between consecutive test distributions, and a label-marginal shift condition. These refine the formal problem assumptions. The STAD model equations, softmax equivalence, and Gaussian/vMF derivations in Appendices A–B otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contribution of tracking last-layer dynamics and the small-batch advantage remain. V2 adds label-shift robustness to the abstract's principal performance claims and presents formalizing TempTTA as a contribution. V1 instead foregrounded the two implementations and improvements over TENT and CoTTA on Wild-Time.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the interpretation of label shift: homogeneous batches strengthen prototype estimation, while imbalanced normalization statistics harm feature adaptation. This refines v1's catastrophic-forgetting explanation for FMoW failures. V2 also softens the dispersion diagnostic from assertions that high dispersion makes STAD sufficient to a potential warning metric, while retaining the representation-quality limitation.

D1.justification: V2 adds algorithmic pseudocode, specifies the previously unspecified default sliding-window size of 3, and tabulates concentration settings by dataset and shift condition. Appendix C also provides implementation details and hyperparameter grids for the four additional baselines and new source architectures. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond relocated descriptions.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges earlier classifier-adaptation approaches, positioning T3A as a close prototype-based predecessor and distinguishing STAD through its dynamics model. Sections 1–4 substantially expand discussion of temporal domain generalization, structured state-space models, and TTA approaches addressing temporal correlation and class imbalance. These are substantive positioning changes beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, problem setting, related work, experimental narrative, and conclusion. Experiments are reorganized around temporal shifts, other shifts, and tracking analysis. Architecture and baseline descriptions move into a reorganized Appendix C, and the appendices gain additional subdivisions.

P2.justification: V1 Figure 1 is separated into v2 Figures 1–2; the combined time/batch-size display becomes expanded Figures 4–5. The dispersion panels are reordered in Figure 6. Tables gain shift-specific columns, method groups, and performance coloring. New comparison, hyperparameter, sensitivity, and visualization displays substantially change the presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important empirical gaps by adding relevant classifier-adaptation competitors and distinguishing the label conditions behind the strong FMoW result. The expanded comparisons, more cautious dispersion interpretation, pseudocode, and explicit window settings substantially improve interpretability and reproducibility. Losing the fixed-proportion imbalance study and leaving the CIFAR setting revision unexplained against retained scores are limitations, but the stronger comparative evidence resolves significant weaknesses in v1.
